Endeavor Catalyst raises $320M for global tech founders.
Evidence: $320M fund raised, 90% non-US investments, nonprofit profit-sharing model.
#TechCrunch #VentureCapital

Endeavor Catalyst closed a $320M fund to back breakthrough tech founders outside Silicon Valley, returning half its profits to support global entrepreneurship.

While backing global founders, the fund operates within an exclusive elite network where 50% profits fund nonprofit operations and elite governance loops.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.6, +0.5) — Conditional Good

A massive fund empowers global founders outside San Francisco, though constrained by traditional elite venture gatekeeping.

Integrity: Trustworthy (Hypocrisy: 1.25, z: 1)

- Fund Allocation: PASS (+0.8, +0.7) — Reaches overseas founders effectively.
- Nonprofit Model: COND (+0.4, +0.3) — Half profits retained by elite network.
Endeavor Catalyst has closed its fifth fund at $320M, bringing total assets past $850M to back tech founders globally outside Silicon Valley hubs.

The Bright Side:
Unprecedented capital access reaches high-growth startups across Europe, Latin America, and emerging markets.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing geographic decentralization (WHERE) with systemic democratization of venture access (WHO).

Endeavor operates a smart altruistic loop by directing capital to overlooked regions, though anchored by elite board members and high screening barriers.

When you map stated global intentions against selective elite filtering, it plots a trajectory toward conditional empowerment.

The Unavoidable Truth: Venture capital can successfully expand beyond Silicon Valley borders.

The Unavoidable Lie: Elite mentorship networks are universally open to any aspiring founder.

Endeavor Catalyst has closed its fifth fund with $320 million in capital commitments, bringing the firm’s total assets under management to more than $850 million. The raise is good news for founders outside the Bay Area who risk getting overlooked as more funds focus squarely on AI companies in Silicon Valley.

Endeavor Catalyst is the venture arm of Endeavor, a New York-based global nonprofit that has spent 30 years supporting founders outside major tech hubs. (It calls all those other places “elsewhere” throughout its marketing materials.)

The fund is run by managing partner Allen Taylor, a 20-year veteran of the organization, and managing director Jackie Carmel, who joined Endeavor Catalyst 12 years ago, along with a 16-person team. The official general partner, though, is Endeavor itself. What that means, says Linda Rottenberg, who co-founded Endeavor and helped start Endeavor Catalyst in 2012, is that “half of the fund’s profits go back to Endeavor, so every investment helps the next generation of founders who are building elsewhere.”

The bar for those founders is pretty high. A person first has to get into Endeavor’s network, where he or she can access Endeavor’s mentoring and extensive network, and that’s hard. Last year, the group says it screened more than 10,000 candidates and picked 88. The network now has more than 3,100 entrepreneurs in over 50 countries.

When one of those founders’ companies raises at least $5 million in a round led by another institutional investor, Endeavor Catalyst can join in on the same terms as that lead. The team tells TechCrunch that checks usually run $1 million to $3 million but can’t exceed 10% of the round.

Over the next few years, they plan to make 40 to 50 investments annually, investing in up to 150 companies altogether with this new fund, they say.

Taylor, via an email exchange, wouldn’t share numbers on cash-on-cash returns tied to its earlier funds, but he did point to some impressive-sounding numbers. Across all five funds, he says, Endeavor Catalyst has backed 437 companies in 44 markets. Eighty-three of those startups are currently valued at $1 billion or more, he says, and the unit has seen 39 exits and 11 IPOs.

Some of the venture arm’s most valuable holdings right now include four-year-old ElevenLabs, the maker of AI voice tools that was recently valued at $22 billion in a secondary sale (it was founded in Poland originally), and Bending Spoons, the 13-year-old Italy-based conglomerate that went public in July and that currently boasts a $26 billion market cap.

Other holdings include New York-based Reflection AI (founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers — one of whom was born in Greece), which is now valued at $25 billion; Checkout.com, whose founder is Swiss and which was valued last year at $12 billion; the African payments infrastructure company Flutterwave, valued this summer at $3.2 billion; and AI coding startup Replit, co-founded by Amjad Masad, who is Palestinian-Jordanian. Replit snagged a $9 billion valuation earlier this year.

Endeavor, the nonprofit, has especially well-connected people associated with it, including board members Reid Hoffman; Nick Beim, a career VC who has spent the last 25 years at Matrix Partners, then Venrock; and Edgar Bronfman Jr., the former head of Warner Music and Seagram, who chairs Endeavor’s board.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis is a longtime friend of Endeavor, too, having gone to Harvard with Rottenberg. (Late last month in San Francisco, I sat down with him during a rare visit to the Bay Area that was organized by Endeavor and where he met with tech founders and Greek expatriates.)

Altogether, Endeavor Catalyst’s newest fund includes 400 limited partners, including Hoffman; famed hedge fund manager Bill Ackman; and the Dutch investment group Prosus. According to Taylor, roughly 30% of those backers are Endeavor founders themselves, including founders of Nubank, Revolut, and Checkout.com.

While so much attention is paid to what’s happening in San Francisco and its immediate environs right now, the bets of Endeavor Catalyst suggest what other investors may be missing, and Endeavor, with local teams and mentors in dozens of countries, seems particularly well-positioned to see it.

Indeed, about 90% of the venture arm’s investments are outside the U.S., it says. Europe is its fastest-growing region, with 12 new investments in the first half of 2026 compared with 14 in all of last year, though Latin America is still the largest.

Repeat founders are also becoming a bigger part of the mix. Taylor tells TechCrunch that roughly 14% of Endeavor Catalyst’s fourth fund went to second companies started by Endeavor founders at the seed or Series A stage. With this new fund, the team expects that number will reach 20%.

Pictured above: Endeavor co-founder Linda Rottenberg onstage in Turin, Italy, earlier this month.
